opening.headline: We find the reason why some requests fail during rolling updates in probe and resource settings, and distinguish between the roles of the three probes and the relationships between requests, limits, and QoS classes.
body: I deployed a new version and some requests are returning errors during the rolling update. Traffic comes in as soon as a new pod is signaled, because while the model file is being read, that pod cannot yet respond to requests. There is a difference between when a pod is started and when it is ready to receive requests. Conversely, if the termination signal and traffic blocking are mismatched on the side where the previous pod was going down, the request in progress is disconnected.

In this class, we first organize the relationships between basic objects such as nodes, pods, kubelets, controllers, and services, and see how Deployment gradually replaces pods. Next, we'll break down what the startup, readiness, and liveness probes each measure, the order of things that happen when a pod terminates, and the graceful shutdown settings. Next, we will look at how requests, limits, and Pod QoS levels are related to eviction decisions when node resources are insufficient, and solve the settings using a service that takes a long time to load models.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of nodes, pods, kubelets, controllers, and services and how the controller matches the declared state.
Can explain what deployment, probes, requests and limits, and QoS levels do
The roles of startup, readiness, and liveness probes can be distinguished.
Explains the pod termination order and the roles of terminationGracePeriodSeconds and preStop, and allows you to select settings to prevent termination side failures during rolling updates.

screens.title: Some requests fail during rolling updates
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow where requests fail as pods are replaced one by one.

visual.alt: A timeline where old pods are replaced with new pods one by one, and requests fail during the model loading section of the new pods.

steps.title: 1. A new pod is started
steps.body: Deployment starts creating a new version of the pod. A Pod is the smallest deployment unit in Kubernetes that bundles one or more containers. Now that the container process has started, the pod is in the Running state. At this point, the model server is still reading the weights file.

steps.title: 2. Traffic comes in right away
steps.body: Without a device to check for readiness, Kubernetes only sees that the container has started and puts a new pod into the service's target. A service is a static access point that sits in front of a set of Pods and has a list of targets to which to send requests. Requests will begin flowing to the new pod.

steps.title: 3. Request fails while loading model
steps.body: The new pod becomes unresponsive while reading the model file. Requests made in between will result in errors due to connection refusal or timeout. Old pods are being replaced and disappearing, so there are fewer places to receive failed requests.

steps.title: 4. Requests are also dropped on the previous pod going down.
steps.body: Failure is not limited to those who start. If the process terminates as soon as it receives a termination signal when the previous pod goes down, any requests that are still being processed will be interrupted. Additionally, the removal of a Pod from a service's target list and the sending of a shutdown signal may occur simultaneously, so new requests may arrive shortly after the shutdown signal. Servers that process longer inference requests have a greater impact on this section.

steps.title: 5. Summary of the problem
steps.body: There are two causes: The starting side did not distinguish between ‘started’ and ‘ready’, and the descending side did not distinguish between ‘started termination’ and ‘completed request’. The separation on the start side is made by the probe, and the separation on the end side is made by the normal shutdown settings. This class covers both sides.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the problem looks like, let's think about a similar experience.

screens.title: Remember: There is a difference between being ready and being ready.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Some requests fail during rolling updates. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: A typical pattern is that the error rate rises briefly immediately after deployment and then subsides. If the errors are limited to the deployment window, you may suspect pre-preparation traffic rather than a code defect.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a difference between when the process started and when you were ready to receive a request?
items.answer: A web server is ready in seconds, but a model server takes tens of seconds to minutes to load weights into memory or the GPU. The slower the start, the larger the gap between the two points in time becomes, making the problem more noticeable.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a container that overused its memory suddenly restart?
items.answer: If the memory limit is exceeded, the kernel will kill the container with OOM. Since model servers have large memory usage and change depending on requests, how the limit is set determines stability.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a long request get cut off midway during deployment?
items.answer: If the previous pod goes down as soon as it receives a shutdown signal, any requests it was processing will be disconnected. This is especially common on model servers where a single request can take tens of seconds. Keep in mind that the setting determines how long to wait after the end signal.

screens.outro: First, let's look at how Deployment replaces pods.

screens.title: Kubernetes basic objects: node, pod, kubelet, controller, service
screens.lead: Select the numbered markers in the picture to see what each component does and how it connects to one another. Deployment, probe, and resource settings on subsequent screens all operate on this structure.

visual.alt: An illustration of the Kubernetes structure where the controller adjusts the declared state, the kubelet on the node runs the pod, and the service forwards the request to the pod list.
labels: Compare the desired state with the current state.

markers.label: node
markers.title: Nodes are the machines on which pods actually run.
markers.body: A node is a working machine in a cluster and can be a physical server or a virtual machine. For a pod to run on a node, the node must have a container runtime. In a GPU service, there are separate nodes with GPUs, and pods are placed on nodes with the necessary resources.

markers.label: pod
markers.title: A pod is the smallest deployment unit of containers.
markers.body: A Pod is the smallest deployment unit in Kubernetes that bundles one or more containers and shares storage and network. Most of them are wrapped around a single container. Pods are a temporary resource, so they are created and destroyed, and each Pod has its own IP address. Therefore, individual pods are not expected to survive for long, and are usually created through a workload resource such as Deployment.

markers.label: kubelet
markers.title: The kubelet runs and watches pods on a node.
markers.body: The kubelet is an agent that runs on each node in the cluster and verifies that the containers listed in the pod specification are running and healthy. It is the kubelet that runs probes, restarts containers based on the results, and sends a shutdown signal to containers when a pod terminates.

markers.label: controller
markers.title: The controller continues to adjust the declared state.
markers.body: The spec of a Kubernetes object contains the desired state. The controller is an iterative loop that continually adapts the current state to this desired state. Setting a heating temperature is like having a thermostat set the actual temperature. Deployment's controller ensures that the number of pods and templates remain as declared, creating new pods when they disappear and replacing them when the template changes.

markers.label: Service
markers.title: A Service is a fixed access point in front of a changing set of Pods.
markers.body: The IP of a pod changes when the pod changes, making it difficult for the client to remember it directly. A Service ties together a set of Pods into a single access point. For Services that have a selector, the control plane automatically creates an EndpointSlice, and this list contains pods that match the condition. Requests are routed to the pods in this list, so when a pod enters or leaves the list, it receives or stops receiving traffic.

screens.outro: Now that we have the structure in order, let's see how Deployment replaces pods.

screens.title: Deployment and rolling updates
screens.lead: Try changing the maxUnavailable value with the slider to see how the replacement order changes the number of pods kept simultaneously.

stops.body: The desired number of pods is always maintained, even during rolling updates. Only after the new pod is ready do you unload the old pod. Instead, you will temporarily have more pods than you want, so you will need as much free resources as maxSurge. This is true when availability is paramount and resources are available.

This is the default. Deployment declares the desired number of pods (replicas) and pod templates, and ReplicaSet maintains that number. Replacing a template creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually replaces old pods with new ones. At this time, the replacement speed is controlled by maxUnavailable and maxSurge. The selector and pod label must match for ReplicaSet to find its pod.

This means that it can be reduced by half at a time, which speeds up replacement but significantly reduces service capacity. In model services where pods take a long time to become ready, this value can increase errors.

If a new version is not available, the controller stops going any further due to maxUnavailable. This safeguard is only meaningful when new pods accurately indicate their readiness status. How to tell if you are ready is the probe we will look at next.

screens.outro: The probes must be accurate to have confidence that the rollout is ready. Let's look at the roles of the three probes.

screens.title: Role of the three probes
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what each probe determines and what happens if it fails.

visual.alt: A timeline showing where startup, readiness, and liveness probes run during the pod's lifetime.

tabs.label: startup probe
tabs.body: Check whether the application inside the container has started. If a startup probe is set, Kubernetes will not run liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds, giving it time to initialize. It only runs on startup, and if it fails, the kubelet kills the container and follows its restart policy. This probe is needed for model servers that take a long time to start.

tabs.label: readiness probe
tabs.body: Decide if you can receive traffic now. If it fails, the pod's IP will be taken out of the service's EndpointSlice, no traffic will go, but the container will not be restarted. Since it runs periodically throughout the life of the container, it is also used to temporarily relieve traffic when it is difficult to receive requests due to temporary overload.

tabs.label: liveness probe
tabs.body: Determine whether the container needs to be restarted. It is intended to catch deadlocks where the application is running but cannot make progress. The kubelet restarts the container if it fails more times than allowed. The document warns to write carefully. If configured incorrectly, this can cause cascading failures that cause containers to restart under high load, increasing the load on the remaining pods.

tabs.label: How to write together
tabs.body: A common pattern is to use the same endpoint for readiness and liveness, but set the failureThreshold for liveness higher. This means that even with the same confirmation, the decision to remove traffic should be made quickly, and the decision to restart should be made more carefully. liveness does not wait for readiness success, so to make it wait, use initialDelaySeconds or startup probe.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the roles, let's follow the probe results and traffic over time.

screens.title: Traffic flow process depending on probe status
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see the probe results and service endpoints change chronologically after the pod starts.

steps.title: 1. The pod starts
steps.body: If the startup probe is set, initially only the startup probe is waited for to pass. During this time, liveness and readiness are not running, and this pod is not in the service's endpoint list.

steps.title: 2. Startup is successful
steps.body: If the startup probe is successful, the liveness and readiness probes are started. This is the signal that the model has finished loading. The startup probe will not run again after this.

steps.title: 3. Readiness is the first success.
steps.body: Only after readiness succeeds for the first time does the pod enter the service endpoint list and traffic begins to flow. Rolling updates require new pods to pass this stage before older pods are moved down, reducing request failures.

steps.title: 4. Readiness leads to failure
steps.body: If readiness fails due to overload or dependent service issues, the pod is ejected from the endpoint. The container will not be restarted, it will just stay there and return to the list if it succeeds again.

steps.title: 5. Liveness continues to fail
steps.body: If liveness fails more than the allowed number of times, the container is restarted and starts from the startup phase again. Meanwhile, the pod is also removed from the endpoint.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the traffic, let's look at resource settings and QoS ratings.

screens.title: What happens when a pod terminates and settings for a graceful shutdown
screens.lead: Use the slider to change the settings of the termination section one by one, and check the path where requests are cut off when the previous pod goes down and the settings that block it.

visual.alt: A timeline where termination signaling and endpoint removal begin simultaneously at the point of pod deletion, and are forced to terminate when the grace period ends.
labels: kubelet: After executing preStop, a termination signal (SIGTERM) is sent, and the app completes the request.
Control Plane: Remove pods from serviced list, change propagates to proxy and load balancer
Grace time ends (default 30 seconds): SIGKILL remaining processes
A section where new requests can arrive even after the end signal

stops.body: When a pod is erased or a rolling update unloads an old pod, two things begin to happen simultaneously. The kubelet sends a termination signal (SIGTERM) to the container, and the control plane begins removing this pod from the service's list of targets (EndpointSlice). Because there is no guaranteed order between the two paths, and list changes take time to propagate through proxies and load balancers, new requests may continue to arrive for some time after the termination signal arrives. If the app terminates the process as soon as it receives the termination signal, that request and any requests it was processing will be disconnected. This is the downside failure in rolling updates. The default value for grace time (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) is 30 seconds.

When the model server receives a termination signal, it does not accept new connections, and if it is configured to terminate the process after finishing ongoing requests, requests will not be interrupted in the middle. This is a long inference request that is generating a token. On the Kubernetes side, the grace time is the upper limit on the time allowed for this finalization. If any processes remain after the grace period, a SIGKILL is sent to the remaining processes, forcing them to terminate. You must first check whether the server supports graceful shutdown in response to a shutdown signal.

The preStop hook is executed before the stop signal is sent, and the stop signal is not sent until the hook ends. If you wait a few seconds here, changes to the target list will have time to propagate, and the server will receive a shutdown signal after no more new requests are coming. There are three types of hooks: executing a command, making an HTTP request, and waiting for a certain amount of time.

```yaml
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90
  containers:
  - name: model-server
    image: my-model-server
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        sleep:
          seconds: 10
```

The example above is a setting that waits 10 seconds before the end signal and increases the total grace time to 90 seconds.

The grace time countdown starts before executing the preStop hook, so the time the hook spends is also subtracted from the same grace time. For example, if the grace time is 60 seconds, the hook takes 55 seconds, and the container needs 10 more seconds to gracefully exit after the shutdown signal, the total will be 65 seconds, which will force the container to exit before it can finish the graceful shutdown. Assuming that a service request takes up to 40 seconds, the grace time should be greater than the hook waiting time plus the longest request's finalization time plus margin. If the hook exceeds the grace time, Kubernetes only allows one 2-second extension, so make this calculation in advance.

In a rolling update, this shutdown process occurs once each time the previous pod is brought down. Setting maxUnavailable to 0 will preserve throughput capacity by lowering old pods only after new pods are ready, but this alone will not solve the problem of dropped requests from pods being dropped. The starting side is blocked by the readiness probe, and the descending side is blocked by normal shutdown processing, preStop, and grace time. Setting up both will eliminate the issue of some requests failing during rolling updates.

screens.title: requests and limits, Pod QoS
screens.lead: Read the table and compare the conditions of the three QoS levels and the eviction order when node resources are insufficient.

data.caption: Pod QoS level conditions and eviction order
rows: Guaranteed
CPU and memory requests and limits are specified for all containers and are the same.
The request limit is clear, but there is no exemption from eviction.
Burstable
Even though it is not guaranteed, one of the containers has requests or limits.
Considering request overflow and Pod priority together
BestEffort
There are no requests or limits in any container
Vulnerable to pressure due to lack of requests; No fixed priority order
data.notes: requests is the guaranteed amount that the scheduler uses when selecting a node, and limits is the upper limit that will be restricted if exceeded. CPU limits slow things down by throttling, but memory limits are enforced by OOM exits in the kernel, so exceeding them can kill the container. When stressing a node, pods that exceed the request are given priority, but pods that write below the request may also be evicted depending on the situation. This difference comes from the way cgroups in the Linux kernel manage resources. The CPU limit is an upper limit that checks the usage time every set time unit and causes the kernel to temporarily stop the execution of the container when the limit is reached. CPU request is used as a weighting factor so that when multiple containers compete for CPU, the larger the request, the more CPU time it receives. On the other hand, memory cannot be reclaimed once allocated, so if an attempt is made to allocate more than the limit, the kernel's OOM processing terminates the process. In other words, the problem can be solved by slowing down the CPU, but the problem must be solved by killing the memory. And since memory limits are enforced when the kernel detects memory pressure, containers that over-allocate may not be terminated immediately. Unlike CPU, expansion resources such as GPU cannot be over-allocated, so only limits must be written or requests and limits must be written the same.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the resource settings, let's look at the remaining objects used to operate the service.

screens.title: Secret, Job and CronJob, Label and Annotation
screens.lead: You can select and expand each item to see how it is used in the model service. Open them all and compare.

items.title: Secret: Inject API key
items.body: Secret passes credentials to the container as an environment variable or file. If you inject your model provider's API key as a Secret rather than putting it in the image, you don't have to rebuild the image when you change the key. Access should be restricted with least privilege RBAC. Secret can also contain credentials to retrieve images from private registries.

items.title: Job and CronJob: Nightly reindex
items.body: Job executes a one-time task, and CronJob creates a job with a schedule in the cron syntax. Ideal for rebuilding search indexes or running evaluation tasks nightly. Unlike service pods, it is normal for them to end, so they are not created as Deployments.

items.title: Labels and Annotations: Team Separation
items.body: Labels are used to select and group objects. Labels are also used as a standard for services to find pods, and are also used to classify teams and environments. Annotations are used to attach additional information that is not used for selection. For example, you can include contact information or model version information.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the components, let's apply it to an example to solve a service with long model loading.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Services with long model loading require a startup probe
screens.lead: It takes 3 minutes to load the model, but the liveness is set to short. Select the right arrow to follow the instructor's solution.

steps.title: setting of the problem
steps.body:
Model loading takes 3 minutes with the following settings:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
```

liveness checks every 10 seconds and restarts the container after 3 failures. These 3 minutes also include downloading time to start with the weights, if any. Since the startup time will vary depending on whether the weights are placed in an image, mounted as a volume, or downloaded at startup, the allowable time should be determined by the value measured by that method.

steps.title: Step 1: What Happens If We Continue?
steps.body: It determines that it is unresponsive within about 30 seconds of startup and kills the container. Model loading cannot be completed as it requires 3 minutes, and when the container is restarted, loading is repeated from the beginning. This will result in a loop of restarts where the pod will never be ready.

steps.title: Step 2: Conditions for placing a startup probe
steps.body: To survive on liveness alone, `initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold × periodSeconds` must be longer than the start time. However, increasing this value also increases the time it takes to detect a deadlock during normal operation. So, if the startup time is longer than this value, the startup probe is set aside.

steps.title: Step 3: Increase the allowable startup time to 3 minutes or more.
steps.body: Set `failureThreshold` of the startup probe to a large size so that `periodSeconds × failureThreshold` exceeds 3 minutes. For example, setting periodSeconds to 10 and failureThreshold to 30 allows up to 5 minutes. You can leave the liveness value as is, because liveness will not be executed until startup is successful.

steps.title: Step 4: Eliminate rolling update errors with readiness
steps.body: The readiness probe ensures that the endpoint succeeds only after the model has finished loading. Then traffic won't go down until the new pod is ready, and the old pod won't go down either because of maxUnavailable. Request failures during rolling updates, which were the initial issue, are eliminated.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: startup protects against slow starts, readiness dictates traffic timing, and liveness catches deadlock after startup. The three probes must be divided into roles to ensure stable deployment of the slow model service.

screens.outro: Next, we will explain the thinking behind choosing resource setup and eviction order.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Thoughts on choosing memory settings and QoS
screens.lead: This is a situation where the inference server and log collector are running on the same node, and the node memory is running low. Select the right arrow to follow the judgment sequence.

steps.title: sorting out the situation
steps.body: You have both an inference server and a log collector on one node, and the node runs out of memory. The kubelet determines the eviction priority based on request exceedance, Pod priority, and relative usage. What we have to decide is which pods we can keep and which we can give up.

steps.title: Step 1: Inference Server is Guaranteed
steps.body: If the requests and limits of the inference server are the same for both CPU and memory, it becomes Guaranteed and resource requests and limits become clear. However, this does not guarantee that you will not be ousted. Instead, it costs money because as many resources as requests are always reserved on the node.

steps.title: Step 2: Leave some room in memory limit
steps.body: If you set the memory limit lower than the actual usage, the kernel will forcefully terminate the container with OOM. Since the model server's memory increases when there is a large number of requests, the maximum usage is measured and the limit is set with some margin.

steps.title: Step 3: Secondary Pod determines whether to accept BestEffort
steps.body: Secondary pods with no configuration become BestEffort and are vulnerable to resource pressure. It determines whether it is okay for the log collector to stop for a while, and if not, makes it burstable by giving the minimum number of requests.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: We intentionally assign Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort in order of importance. Grades should not be left to chance, but should be chosen as a setting.

screens.outro: Let me summarize the key points by combining the two cases.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Signals of readiness and commitment of resources
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: Deployment maintains its declared state and gradually replaces pods with rolling updates. The replacement rate is controlled by maxUnavailable and maxSurge, and the controller stops rolling out new pods if they are not ready.

Startup indicates that the startup has completed, readiness indicates that traffic can be received, and liveness determines whether to restart. The three probes must be divided into roles so that rolling updates of the slow model service can proceed without errors.

When a Pod is terminated, signaling its termination and removing it from the serviced list begin simultaneously. To terminate an ongoing request, the server must terminate gracefully in response to a termination signal, ensure propagation time with preStop, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds larger than the hook time and the finalization time of the longest request.

requests is the guaranteed amount and limits is the upper limit, and QoS alone does not determine the order of eviction during node pressure. Secret is used for minimum privileges, Job and CronJob are used for one-time and periodic tasks, and Labels are used for selection and grouping.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Running means it has started and Ready means it can receive traffic. What connects the two states is the probe.

data.notes: Even if the symptoms are the same, there may be multiple causes. One probe per role and intentional resource settings based on importance should be used to reduce the symptoms in the table above.

glossary.def: A controller is an iterative loop that continuously adjusts the current state to the declared state. Deployment maintains the number of pods and templates you declare, and replaces them with rolling updates.
A probe that determines whether traffic is acceptable to receive and whether to include it in the service endpoint.
A probe that determines whether a container needs to be restarted. Consecutive failures cause the kubelet to restart.
This is a probe that verifies that the application inside the container has started. No other probes will run until it succeeds.

Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort levels are determined by the relationship between requests and limits. Vulnerability can be assessed when a node is pressured, but the actual eviction order is based on both usage and priority.

This is the amount of time allowed for containers that received a shutdown signal when a Pod terminates to finish any work in progress. Set by terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which defaults to 30 seconds and includes the preStop hook execution time.

misconceptions.myth: If the Pod is Running, it can receive requests.
misconceptions.fact: Running means the container has started. It must pass the readiness probe to enter the service endpoint and receive traffic.

misconceptions.myth: The tighter the liveness, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: If liveness is too sensitive, slow startup or high load can be considered a failure, killing containers and creating cascading failures. Slow startup requires a startup probe.

misconceptions.myth: As long as you set the limits large, resources are guaranteed.
misconceptions.fact: The guarantee is provided by requests. Limits are just upper limits that are restricted when exceeded, and if the memory limit is exceeded, it may end with OOM.

misconceptions.myth: Pods that have received a shutdown signal will no longer receive new requests.
misconceptions.fact: Termination signaling and removal from the serviced list begin simultaneously, and list changes take time to propagate. Since new requests may come in the meantime, you must set a waiting time with preStop and allow ongoing requests to finish within the grace period.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Deployment gradually replaces pods with rolling updates.
The three probes have different roles: determining whether startup is complete, traffic is available, or restart.
Requests are guaranteed, limits are the upper limit, and the actual eviction ranking depends on whether requests are exceeded, Pod priority, and relative usage.
Slow model loading requires a combination of startup probes and readiness probes.
When terminating a pod, set normal shutdown processing, preStop, and grace time to ensure that ongoing requests are not interrupted.

checks.explain: Because liveness counts failures and restarts before the loading is finished, we allow 3 minutes for the startup probe to run without any other probes running before the startup is finished.

wrong.0: Lowering the limit only increases the risk of OOM.
wrong.1: A readiness failure only removes the endpoint and does not cause it to restart.
wrong.2: QoS and eviction are not the cause of this symptom.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. The results will not be recorded, so feel free to choose.
